799.title: Abu Bakr
799.hook: his closest friend, companion in the cave, who believed him when others called it a lie
799.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Bakr as the Prophet's companion in the cave; Sunni Muslims honor him as the first caliph and call him as-Siddiq, while Shia Muslims view the succession after the Prophet differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sahabi, a companion, anyone who met the Prophet as a believer and died a believer. Your line was the ones who were there.

Medina, the day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has died. The news is out, and the mosque is in uproar. Umar is on his feet, insisting it can't be true. Then a man rides in from his home at as-Sunh, on the edge of town. He speaks to no one. He goes straight into Aisha's room, uncovers the Prophet's face, and kisses him. Then he walks out to the crowd, and everyone waits to hear what the closest friend will say. His name is Abu Bakr.
screen: `THE MOSQUE IN UPROAR.` → `A MAN RIDES IN.` → `HE KISSES HIS FRIEND'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records what he said. Whoever worshipped Muhammad: Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah: Allah is alive and does not die. Then he recited a verse from Surah Al Imran, in Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him." The report says it was as if people had never heard the verse until he recited it, and soon everyone was saying it. Umar said later that when he heard it, his legs gave way beneath him. So who was this man, steady enough to hold a whole city on that day? Earlier this year we heard the Prophet defend him in a quarrel, in Bukhari: when Allah sent me to you, you said, you are lying, and Abu Bakr said, he has told the truth, and he stood by me with himself and his wealth. Will you leave my companion alone? The tradition calls him as-Siddiq, the one who affirms the truth. In another report, the Prophet said that if he were to take an intimate friend other than his Lord, it would be Abu Bakr. Then there is the cave. The Qur'an calls the Prophet the second of two, hiding with one companion, and commentators name that companion Abu Bakr. After the Prophet's death, the community chose Abu Bakr as caliph, to lead it. Sunni Muslims honor him as the first of the rightly guided caliphs. Shia Muslims hold that leadership belonged to Ali, and remember these days differently. The verse he recited is the same for both.

segments.voice: Think of a friend who is carrying something right now: a loss, a fear, a project nobody else believes in. Loyalty is usually small, a visit, a message that says I believe you, simply showing up when others drift away, so let one small thing come to mind for them. If you pray, ask Allah to make you a good companion to them.
Abu Bakr. The Prophet's close friend and companion in the cave, called as-Siddiq for affirming him when others called him a liar. Today's word.
Your line: the second of two. The friend who stays steady when the city shakes. Seven hundred ninety-nine days in.

800.title: Abu Bakr's purchases
800.hook: he spends his wealth buying freedom for enslaved believers, Bilal among them
800.howItsDone: Islamic law counts freeing a captive or slave as a great good deed and an expiation for some sins, and some Muslims today direct charity toward people trapped in debt or in need of release.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Bakr, as-Siddiq, who said he has told the truth when others said you lie. Your line was the second of two.

Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master. That's Umar talking, in a report in Bukhari, and the second master is Bilal. We met Bilal earlier this year, pinned under a stone in the Meccan heat, saying only: One. One. We saw Abu Bakr buy him and set him free. Today the camera turns around, from the man under the stone to the man with the purse, and to the others he paid for. Today: Abu Bakr's purchases.
screen: `OUR MASTER FREED OUR MASTER.` → `BILAL, UNDER THE STONE.` → `THE MAN WITH THE PURSE.`

segments.voice: Look at Umar's sentence again. Sayyid, master, is a word for the powerful, and Umar uses it twice. Abu Bakr, the wealthy merchant, is our master. And Bilal, the man who was bought, is our master too. The voice that called the prayer in Medina had once been property. Bilal was not the only one. The sirah tells of other enslaved believers, women and men, whom Abu Bakr bought and freed while the Muslims in Mecca were still few and weak. It also tells a small scene at home. His father, Abu Quhafa, said to him: my son, you are freeing weak people. If you must free someone, free strong men who could protect you. Abu Bakr answered that he was doing it for the sake of Allah alone. Commentators connect this to verses at the end of Surah al-Layl. In paraphrase: the one who gives his wealth to grow in goodness, who isn't paying back a favor anyone did him, but seeks only the face of his Lord Most High, will be content. Freeing someone is not a side note in the Qur'an. In Surah al-Balad, the steep road a person is told to climb is described as freeing a neck, fakk raqabah, the Qur'an's phrase for releasing a captive or a slave, or feeding someone on a day of hunger. So when Abu Bakr spent his money, he wasn't buying a name or a bodyguard. He was buying freedom, and getting nothing back that anyone could count.

segments.voice: Freedom comes in many sizes: a debt someone can't climb out of, a fee standing between them and a course, a visa, a fresh start, a caregiver who never gets an afternoon off. 801.title: Umar, al-Faruq
801.hook: fierce, just, the one who distinguishes right and wrong
801.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Umar ibn al-Khattab as the second caliph and tell stories of his justice, while Shia Muslims view his role in the succession differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fakk raqabah, freeing a neck, and Abu Bakr spending his wealth on Bilal and others. Your line was buying freedom.

Near the Ka'ba is a spot the Qur'an calls the place where Abraham stood. Umar once said to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: why don't we take the place where Abraham stood as a place of prayer? And then, Umar says in Bukhari, a verse came down. In Pickthall's words: "Take as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray)." Pilgrims still pray there. Umar had his own way of putting it: my Lord agreed with me. Today: the man they called al-Faruq.
screen: `THE PLACE WHERE ABRAHAM STOOD.` → `UMAR ASKS.` → `MY LORD AGREED WITH ME.`

segments.voice: In that report, Umar names three things where, he said, his Lord agreed with him: the place of prayer by Abraham's stone, the screening of the Prophet's wives, and a warning to them in a quarrel at home. He isn't boasting. He is remembering moments when what he thought was fair and what was revealed turned out to match. Al-Faruq means the one who distinguishes, who separates true from false, right from wrong. Sources differ on who first called him that. The Prophet said striking things about him. In one report in Bukhari, he tells Umar that whenever Satan meets him on a road, Satan takes a different road. In another, he says that earlier nations had people who were inspired, and if there were one in his community, it would be Umar. This is the same Umar who, in Ibn Ishaq's telling, had once set out to harm the Prophet, and then came into Islam himself. The fierceness didn't go away. It got pointed in a new direction. Later, as caliph, he was remembered as a judge. A letter on judging is attributed to him, telling a governor to treat people equally: in how you look at them, where you seat them, and how you rule, so the powerful don't hope you'll lean their way and the weak don't lose hope in your fairness. Sunni Muslims honor Umar as the second caliph. Shia Muslims view his part in the succession differently, and remember him in another light. What the name al-Faruq asks of anyone is plain: see the difference, then act on it.

802.title: Umar's night walks
802.hook: as caliph he walks at night and carries flour on his own back to a hungry family (reported)
802.howItsDone: Muslims tell stories of Umar's night walks as examples of a ruler's responsibility, and often pair them with the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for those in their care.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Faruq, Umar, the one who tells right from wrong, and a letter about seating the strong and weak alike. Your line was the one who distinguished.

A fire, far out past the edge of Medina, in the dark. Two men walk toward it: Umar, now the caliph, the leader of the whole community, and Aslam, who served him. This story isn't in Bukhari or Muslim. It's reported in later histories, told on Aslam's authority, and Muslims have passed it on for a long time. At the fire they find a woman and her children. The children are crying. A pot is bubbling on the flames. Today: Umar's night walks.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE DARK.` → `THE CALIPH AND HIS SERVANT.` → `CHILDREN CRYING BY A POT.`

segments.voice: Umar asks what's in the pot. Water, she says. Only water. She's stirring it so the children will think food is coming, until they cry themselves to sleep. Then, not knowing who she's talking to, she says: Allah will judge between us and Umar. He's in charge of us, and he doesn't even know. Umar doesn't argue. He walks back to Medina, to the storehouse, and takes out flour and fat. Put it on my back, he tells Aslam. Aslam offers to carry it for him, and Umar answers with a question: will you carry my burden for me on the Day of Resurrection? So the ruler carries the flour out into the dark, on his own back. In the report, he cooks for them himself, kneeling and blowing on the fire, until the food is ready and the children eat, and he stays until they're laughing and settle down. The woman, still not knowing, tells him he's more fit for the job than the caliph. Whatever you make of the details, the story is built on something that is in Bukhari. The Prophet said that each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler is a shepherd over his people. A man is a shepherd over his household, a woman in her husband's house. Umar heard the woman's line as a charge he would answer for, and the night walk was his answer. Shepherds don't wait in the tent to be told a sheep is lost.

segments.voice: Think about your own small flock, the people who depend on you even a little: a child, a parent, a team, a neighbor, a friend going through it. 803.title: Uthman, the modest
803.hook: gentle and generous, called the possessor of two lights for marrying two of the Prophet's daughters
803.howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya', modesty and inner tact, as part of faith, and often hold up Uthman ibn Affan as its example; Sunni Muslims honor him as the third caliph.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umar's night walks, the caliph with a sack of flour on his back, out in the dark. Your line was the ruler carried the flour.

Aisha tells it, in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down at home, relaxed, his garment pulled up a little from his leg. A knock. Abu Bakr asks to come in. He's welcomed, the Prophet stays just as he is, and they talk. Another knock: Umar. Same thing. He comes in, they talk, nothing changes. A third knock, and this time the Prophet sits up and straightens his clothes before the visitor enters. Aisha notices, and afterward she asks him why. The visitor was Uthman.
screen: `A KNOCK: ABU BAKR.` → `A KNOCK: UMAR.` → `A KNOCK, AND HE SITS UP.`

segments.voice: His answer to Aisha, in the report: shall I not be shy before a man the angels are shy before? The word behind that is haya'. In English it gets translated as modesty, shyness, or bashfulness, but none of those quite fits. Haya' is a kind of inner tact: a sense of what is fitting before God and before people, and a reluctance to cross that line. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet says that haya' is a branch of faith, and in another, that haya' brings nothing but good. So when he straightens his clothes for Uthman, he is meeting a modest man with modesty. Uthman ibn Affan was a wealthy merchant from Mecca, remembered as a gentle one. Tradition gives him a second name: Dhu al-Nurayn, the one with two lights. The usual explanation is that he married two of the Prophet's daughters, Ruqayyah, and after her death, Umm Kulthum. He was generous, too, and his generosity had the same quiet shape. On another day this path saw him equip an army. Tomorrow, a well. Later he became the third caliph, honored by Sunni Muslims among the rightly guided caliphs, while Shia Muslims view the succession differently. But the scene this tradition keeps is small. Not a battle, not a speech. A man so modest that even the Prophet sat up when he knocked.

804.title: The well of Rumah
804.hook: Uthman buys a well and makes its water free for all (Tirmidhi)
804.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, by funding wells, schools, mosques and other endowments (waqf), often in the name of someone who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uthman, the knock that made the Prophet sit up, and haya', modesty, a branch of faith. Your line was the modest one.

A bucket on a rope. That's the whole image of today's story. In a report in Tirmidhi, Uthman recalls the early days in Medina. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to the city, Uthman says, there was no sweet water to drink except one well, called Rumah, and it had an owner. The Prophet asked: who will buy the well of Rumah and put his bucket in it alongside the buckets of the Muslims, for something better than it in Paradise? Uthman bought it, he says, with his own money. Today: the well of Rumah.
screen: `ONE WELL OF SWEET WATER.` → `WHO WILL BUY IT?` → `UTHMAN BUYS IT.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the Prophet phrased it. Not: who will buy the well and own it. Not: who will buy it and hand out water to the poor. Who will put his bucket alongside the buckets of the Muslims. The owner's bucket goes down the same shaft as everyone else's: no private rope, no first turn, no gate. Uthman pays, and from then on he drinks the way the poorest person in Medina drinks. Bukhari mentions this well too, in a chapter on endowments, which is where Muslim jurists place gifts like it. Some gifts are spent once: a meal, a coin. Others keep giving after you hand them over. A well. A shade tree. A school. Muslims call this sadaqah jariyah, flowing charity, charity that keeps running like water. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except three: a flowing charity, knowledge that people benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. Now the hard part of Tirmidhi's report. Uthman tells this story much later, when he is caliph and rebels have him shut up in his own house. He reminds them of the well he bought for everyone, and says that now they won't let him drink from it. The water he set free kept flowing to the very people who turned against him, while, in the report, he was left drinking salty water inside. Once he had made it free, it was free for everyone.

805.title: Ali ibn Abi Talib
805.hook: the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, brave, learned and plain-living
805.howItsDone: Muslims honor Ali ibn Abi Talib; Sunni Muslims count him the fourth caliph, and Shia Muslims hold him to be the first Imam, the Prophet's rightful successor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the well of Rumah, Uthman's bucket going down alongside everyone else's. Your line was free water.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes to his daughter Fatimah's house and asks where her husband is. They had words, she says, and he went out. The Prophet sends a man to look, and word comes back: he's asleep in the mosque. So the Prophet goes to him, and finds him on the floor, his cloak slipped off and his side covered in dust. He sits down and wipes the dust off him, saying: get up, Abu Turab. Get up, father of dust. The man on the floor is Ali, his cousin. The narrator in Bukhari adds: of all his names, it was the one Ali loved best.
screen: `THEY HAD WORDS.` → `ASLEEP IN THE DUST.` → `GET UP, ABU TURAB.`

segments.voice: Ali ibn Abi Talib was the son of Abu Talib, the uncle who raised and protected the Prophet. Ibn Ishaq tells that he grew up in the Prophet's house, and he later married his daughter Fatimah: family twice over, cousin and son-in-law. And he was remembered as the lion. At Khaybar, Sahih Muslim reports, he went out to fight singing a line about himself: I am the one my mother named Haydar. Haydar is a name for a lion, and tradition also calls him the lion of God. But the tradition pairs that courage with learning. When the Prophet left him behind in Medina during the march to Tabuk, Ali was upset to stay with the women and children. And the Prophet said, in Bukhari: are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me? Another hadith, in Tirmidhi, has the Prophet say: I am the house of wisdom, and Ali is its door. Scholars debate its chain, and Shia Muslims hold it dear. Then there's the plain living. Abu Turab, father of dust, was a teasing name for a man asleep on a mosque floor, and he loved it. Here is where Muslims differ. Sunni Muslims honor Ali as the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs. Shia Muslims hold him to be the first Imam, the rightful leader after the Prophet. Both honor him. A week that opened with Abu Bakr in the mosque ends with Ali asleep on its floor.
